papers.title: How well does graph superoptimization transfer? Adapting tensor-graph superoptimizer to a Triton-based NPU
papers.abstract: For automatic optimization systems, performance portability across increasingly diverse AI accelerators remains a challenge. We investigate how well graph-level superoptimization transfers across architectures by adapting Mirage from its CUDA-oriented design to the Huawei Ascend 910B3 through a Triton-based compilation stack. We evaluate the adapted system on transformer-relevant workloads, including matrix multiplication, softmax, RMSNorm+MatMul, gated MLP, FNN, and attention. The results show that graph-level optimization can successfully transfer and outperform available reference implementations by up to 87.0% on fused workloads. However, performance is highly dependent on tensor shape and workload structure, with substantial regressions for other configurations. We identify target-specific tensor partitioning, execution-resource modeling, backend lowering and fusion, and search and verification costs as key limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a portable graph representation and programming model do not imply a portable optimization space, motivating modular target-specific mechanisms within otherwise reusable compiler infrastructure.

papers.title: RustMC: Automated Verification of Real-World Concurrent Rust
papers.abstract: RustMC is a stateless model checker that targets push-button verification of unmodified concurrent Rust programs. As both Rust and C/C++ compile to LLVM IR, RustMC builds on GenMC which provides a verification framework for LLVM IR. This allows verification of Rust code and any foreign function dependencies. In this tool paper we present key implementation challenges, use-cases, and an empirical evaluation of RustMC. The challenges include intercepting threading operations, promoting memory intrinsics, and handling uninitialised accesses, all stemming from Rust's unique compilation strategy. Case studies adapted from real-world programs show RustMC finds concurrency bugs in unsafe Rust code, FFI calls to C/C++, and atomic operations. We evaluate our tool's functionality on the Loom model checker test suite and a set of production-level Rust concurrent data structures.

papers.title: Logical Relations on Display
papers.abstract: The metatheory of programming languages suffers from a lack of reuse. Researchers develop individual calculi and prove standard properties, but very few results are truly reused across papers. The problem is worse in proof assistants, where developments routinely duplicate code from prior work or rebuild it from scratch. Category theory provides the most promising path toward reusable programming language semantics. Universal properties capture the type connectives---products, functions, sums---together with their $\beta$/$\eta$ laws. Free categorical structures identify syntactic calculi. \emph{Displayed} categories provide a uniform language for specifying logical relations, and general theorems about fibrations allow their structure to be assembled compositionally. In this work we develop a library of formalized category theory in the Cubical Agda proof assistant directly applicable to programming language metatheory. We develop theories of universal properties and free categorical structures, apply them to define denotational semantics and logical relations for simply typed calculi, and identify encodings of the categorical constructions that make typechecking them tractable. From the same categorical components, we construct several familiar results via a logical relations construction---canonicity,parametricity,conservativity---and provide a proof of coherence for monoidal categories.

papers.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues. In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.

papers.title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
papers.abstract: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.

papers.title: A Unifying Metatheorem on Weak-Memory Robustness
papers.abstract: Memory models specify the behaviors that concurrent programs may exhibit under compiler and hardware optimizations, which often deviate from Sequential Consistency (SC). Robustness is the property of a program P not exhibiting any weak behaviors when executing under a weak memory model MM, compared to SC. As such, the algorithmic problem of deciding whether $P$ is robust against MM has been studied extensively, and has been repeatedly shown to be in PSPACE for many memory models, such as TSO, PSO, and Release/Acquire. However, each model has required its own, dedicated proof, raising the natural question of whether robustness admits a unifying treatment across memory models. In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for a broad class of memory models definable in Kleene Algebra with Tests (KAT). We prove that robustness against any prefix-closed, KAT-definable memory model is in PSPACE. This metatheorem recovers nearly all prior PSPACE robustness results, and establishes PSPACE membership for several new models, including the full RC11 and the OCaml memory model. We have further formalized the correctness of our approach in Lean. On the other hand, we prove that robustness against the KAT-definable Relaxed model is undecidable, and thus prefix-closedness cannot be dropped, in general. Finally, we implement our algorithm in a prototype tool RoboKAT, and demonstrate its flexibility by checking robustness against nine memory models, several of which are not handled by prior work.

papers.title: Simulating Quantum Computation Using Probabilistic Programming
papers.abstract: Developing quantum programs requires not only running them on quantum hardware but also simulating them on classical hardware. Because the meaning of a quantum program can be defined in terms of state vectors, it can be viewed as a form of weighted nondeterminism and simulated using any implementation of probabilistic programming that supports complex or at least negative weights. In this study, we compile a high-level quantum programming language to one such implementation of probabilistic programming, a solver for factor graph grammars. We also extend the solver with an optimization that commutes the tensor operations $\mathsf{einsum}$ and $\mathsf{expand}$. We prove that the compiler and the optimization preserve the denotational semantics of the source language. We perform benchmarks that show our straightforward implementation, by repurposing existing infrastructure for probabilistic programming, attains simulation performance in the ballpark of several other quantum simulators.

papers.title: A Compilation Model for Divergent Parallel Workloads
papers.abstract: Efficient execution on modern parallel machines requires more than abundant parallelism; it demands instruction coherence, memory coherence, and load balance to maximize SIMD utilization and memory bandwidth. Efficiently mapping \textit{divergent} parallel workloads to modern machines, where control flow, memory accesses, and unbounded iteration depend on per-thread runtime values, often requires global program restructuring that trades off increased coherence with reduced locality, parallelism, or extra work. We observe that the key optimizations used to accelerate divergent parallel programs can be expressed as compositions of well-known program transformations from the functional programming and loop optimization communities. We operationalize this insight through \textit{parallel dispatch graphs}: a compilation model that represents divergent programs by representing control flow, data flow between logical stages, and parallel loops within a single abstraction. To facilitate rapid exploration of points in the optimization space, we provide a scheduling language that includes composable transformations of data-dependent control flow and data flow, together with standard loop transformations and hardware bindings. This separation of concerns allows the core algorithm to remain portable, while the execution schedule can be specialized to the specifics of target hardware and input data values. We evaluate our system using popular applications from the domain of spatial computing, and show that the optimization strategies of hand-optimized parallel tree traversals, path tracers, and Monte Carlo PDE solvers can be reproduced as schedules in our system. Our generated code matches or outperforms the hand-optimized implementations (geomeans $1.02$--$2.95\times$ faster). Additionally, we demonstrate empirically that the best schedule varies across programs, machines, and inputs.

papers.title: Datatypes In, Zippers Out!
papers.abstract: A zipper represents a focused position in an algebraic data structure together with the context needed to reconstruct the whole. Datatype derivatives determine one-hole context types, but do not by themselves choose a zipper's concrete representation or specify navigation costs and demands. We present Kamot, a tool that converts regular algebraic datatype declarations in a restricted Haskell fragment into zipper implementations with operational contracts. Navigation, replacement, and reconstruction are proved correct against a reference traversal. Kamot supports mutual recursion and regular containers inside containers. A compositional analysis derives sound bounds on transitions and constructor demands for certified traversal directions. These bounds are affine in trail depth (the number of saved frames) and guarantee termination of each move on productive, potentially infinite inputs. For inhabited families the analysis is complete: when no move certificate is emitted, no bound depending only on trail depth exists, and some productive input makes a move diverge. We prove that the generated code preserves results and the reference order of constructor matches, including finite prefixes of divergent searches. Lean 4 verifies simulation, bounds, and completeness for finite values of single self-recursive datatypes, in both directions. On 19 datatype models and 81 generated families, every generated module passes Haskell type checking, and independent checkers validate certificates, traces, and bounds. In a prefetching workload, starting only searches whose bounds fit a budget answers every local query and avoids discarded source evaluations on long returns, but conservative bounds can lose answers that fuelled search delivers.

papers.title: Statically Typed Purely Functional Definitional Interpreters for {\it Essentials of Programming Languages}
papers.abstract: Definitional interpreters provide an executable and pedagogically effective way to explain programming language semantics. However, when implemented in a dynamically typed and effectful metalanguage, semantic components such as stores, continuations, handlers, substitutions, and scheduling states may remain implicit in the host-language implementation, making it harder to see how language extensions affect interpreter structure. This paper reconstructs the family of interpreters from \textit{Essentials of Programming Languages} (EOPL) in Haskell, a statically typed and purely functional metalanguage, for pedagogical use. We preserve the object languages, examples, and tests of EOPL while making their semantic components explicit through algebraic data types, evaluator signatures, and explicit semantic domains. Across 15 interpreters and 6 type checkers, language extensions are exposed as systematic type-directed changes. The reconstruction is currently used in undergraduate and graduate programming language courses, where students learn interpreter construction through incremental and test-driven development. We further illustrate its pedagogical use through three case studies that progressively extend students' experience: composing mutable state and exception handling, deriving an actor-based interpreter from the typed structure of the EOPL thread interpreter, and translating the CHECKED interpreter and type checker into Rocq to mechanize type safety. Together, the classroom experience and case studies suggest that the reconstruction provides a concrete bridge from learning programming language concepts through executable interpreters to language design and mechanized reasoning.

papers.title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logic for Computer Science
papers.abstract: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logic for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 17 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.3% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.

papers.title: Step in Tine: Forking Processes in Functional Choreographies
papers.abstract: Choreographic programming allows a concurrent programmer to write one centralized program and compile it to individual programs for each system participant. This approach simplifies critical properties like deadlock freedom, but it complicates forking new processes, a core concurrent primitive. This work addresses that gap with the choreographic fork calculus $\lambda{\pitchfork}$, the first functional choreographic language with process spawning. $\lambda{\pitchfork}$ provides a deadlock-freedom guarantee while allowing programs to dynamically determine when to spawn new processes, what they will do, and who will communicate with them. All results are formalized in Lean.

papers.title: Warpline: Binary-Level Tracing and Unified Evidence for Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization
papers.abstract: LLM agents are becoming GPU kernel engineers, but they still tune kernels without seeing where the time goes. Hardware profilers report how busy each unit was, not where each warp's time went; intra-kernel tracers can show it, but only with hand-placed probes and a recompilation that alters the very kernel being measured. We present Warpline, which gives agents this view automatically while leaving the kernel essentially unchanged. Warpline analyzes the binary to decide which events to record and inserts probes into the binary itself without recompilation or any manual step. It then aligns the trace with hardware profiling data on one unified timeline. Because it needs only the binary, it can regenerate this evidence for every new version of the kernel at whatever level the agent edits it (source, IR, or PTX), closing the optimization loop without human intervention. On NVIDIA B200, across 35 kernels in Triton, CuTe DSL, and CUDA C++, Warpline adds a median overhead of 1.2% and leaves a median 99.9% of executed instructions unchanged, whereas existing tracers have median overheads of 1.6% to 13.2% and leave only 4.6% to 32.7% unchanged. Warpline also traces closed-source kernels, which these tracers cannot. On 10 SOL-ExecBench problems, agents using Warpline spend less time and fewer model requests than a bare coding agent and NVIDIA's Kernel Design Agents (KDA), yet lead both after every round in geometric mean and reach a 7.69$\times$ geometric-mean speedup, against 6.94$\times$ and 6.13$\times$. Two case studies further demonstrate that Warpline reveals hidden bottlenecks and provides actionable optimization insights.
